extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral psychology, epistemology, and early-modern philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts conceptual criteria and evaluative distinctions for knowledge, reasoning, passions, and intellectual virtues as presented in an early-modern philosophical treatise. Useful for judging whether thinking, speech, or actions instantiate science, prudence, or particular passions and virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science (definition and method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Science is not Sense or Memory nor merely experience-based Prudence; it is attained by industry: first in apt imposing of Names; secondly by getting a good and orderly Method proceeding from the Elements (which are Names) to Assertions, thence to syllogismes, and so to a knowledge of all the Consequences of names appertaining to the subject in hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science is the knowledge of Consequences and dependance of one fact upon another, enabling one to reproduce effects when like causes are in our power. Contrast with Sense/Memory (knowledge of fact) and Prudence (knowledge by experience).

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of Science
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain signs: when he that pretendeth the Science of any thing can teach the same, i.e., demonstrate the truth perspicuously to another. Uncertain signs: when only some particular events answer to his pretence and many occasions prove so as he says they must.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching/demonstration is an infallible sign; mere success on particular occasions is an uncertain sign. Prudence's signs are all uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence versus Sapience
rubrics_metrics.description: Prudence arises chiefly from much experience; Sapience arises from much science. Both are useful, but Sapience (science-backed ability) is more reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a naturally dextrous swordsman (prudence) vs one who has scientific knowledge of fencing positions (sapience). Beware of relying only on authority or false rules (pedantry) which can lead to disaster.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedantry as anti-pattern (forsaking natural judgement)
rubrics_metrics.description: In business where one lacks infallible science, to forsake one's natural judgement and be guided by general sentences read in authors (subject to many exceptions) is a sign of folly, commonly scorned as Pedantry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even those who display learned reading in public affairs often rely on private prudence in personal matters; show caution when following general rules without attending to particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion: Vital vs Animal (voluntary motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Animals have two sorts of motion: Vitall (continuing bodily functions) and Animal or Voluntary Motion (walking, speaking, moving limbs) which depend on Imagination; voluntary motions have an internal beginning called Endeavour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntary actions presuppose imagination of 'Whither, Which Way, and What'. Small internal beginnings of motion (endeavours) precede observable action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endeavour, Appetite, Aversion (definitions of basic passions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Endeavour toward something that causes it is called APPETITE or DESIRE; endeavour away from something is AVERSION. Desire = Love when object absent; Love = presence; Aversion = Hate when present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appetite often used for hunger/thirst; many appetites derive from experience; we cannot desire what we do not conceive or believe to exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contempt (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: CONTEMPT is an immobility or contumacy of the Heart in resisting the action of certain things; it proceeds from the Heart being already moved otherwise or from want of experience of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Things neither desired nor hated are contemned. Because bodily constitution changes, consistent appetites/aversions across people are impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good and Evil are relative to the person
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatsoever is the object of any man's Appetite or Desire, that is he calls Good; the object of his Hate and Aversion, Evil. There is nothing simply and absolutely Good or Evil; the judgment is relative to the person, commonwealth representative, or an arbitrator agreed upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral language (good/evil/contemptible) is relational; absent a common authority, goodness derives from individual appetites and desires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pulchrum / Turpe; three kinds of Good (promise, effect, means)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pulchrum (Latin) signifies that which by apparent signs promises Good (Good in Promise). Jucundum is Good in Effect (the desired end, delightfull). Utile is Good as Means (Profitable). Corresponding evils: Turpe (promise of evil), Molestum (evil in effect), Inutile (evil as means).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different English words capture facets (beautiful, agreeable, useful). Distinguish Good in promise, Good in effect, Good as means when evaluating objects/actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delight and Displeasure as appearances of appetite
rubrics_metrics.description: The internal motion (appetite) appears to the mind as DELIGHT (when toward) or TROUBLE/OFFENCE (when from). Pleasure (delight) seems to corroborate vital motion and be a help thereto; molestation/displeasure hinders vital motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All appetite/desire/love accompanies some delight; hatred/aversion accompanies some displeasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasures of Sense vs Pleasures of the Mind (Joy, Pain, Grief)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures arising from present sensation (sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch, bodily operations) are Pleasures of Sense. Pleasures arising from expectation/foresight of ends are Pleasures of the Mind, generally called JOY. Displeasures in sense are PAYNE; in expectation are GRIEF.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish immediate sensory pleasure from reflective pleasure (joy). Law-driven moral language ('sensual') is reserved for later discussions of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hope and Despair (appetite with/without opinion of attaining)
rubrics_metrics.description: HOPE: Appetite with an opinion of attaining. DESPAIRE: Appetite without such an opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hope involves belief in possibility; despair is the absence of that belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear and Courage (appraisal with opinion of hurt / avoidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: FEARE: Aversion with opinion of hurt from the object. COURAGE: Aversion combined with hope of avoiding that hurt by resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courage is fear transformed by expectation of successful resistance; anger is sudden courage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anger (sudden courage)
rubrics_metrics.description: ANGER is sudden Courage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anger arises when hope of avoiding harm is immediately available or imagined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence and Diffidence (persistent hope/despair about oneself)
rubrics_metrics.description: CONFIDENCE: Constant Hope of ourselves. DIFFIDENCE: Constant Despair of ourselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confidence grounds attempts; diffidence blocks them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indignation (anger on behalf of another)
rubrics_metrics.description: INDIGNATION: Anger for great hurt done to another, conceived as done by Injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A social/justice-oriented form of anger tied to perceived wrongs to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benevolence (desire of good to another)
rubrics_metrics.description: BENEVOLENCE, GOOD WILL, CHARITY: Desire of good to another. If toward humanity in general, called GOOD NATURE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive other-regarding appetite; names vary with scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covetousness (desire of riches) and Ambition (desire of office)
rubrics_metrics.description: COVETOUSNESSE: Desire of Riches (typically used pejoratively because of contention it causes). AMBITION: Desire of Office or precedence (also often used in worse sense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The moral appraisal of these passions depends on means and social consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pusillanimity and Magnanimity (scale of concern)
rubrics_metrics.description: PUSILLANIMITY: Desire of things that conduce but little to our ends and fear of minor hindrances. MAGNANIMITY: Contempt of little helps and hindrances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnanimity is admirable; pusillanimity is blameworthy. In danger of death, magnanimity becomes Valour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valour (magnanimity under mortal danger)
rubrics_metrics.description: VALOUR / FORTITUDE: Magnanimity in danger of Death or Wounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specific excellence of magnanimity when facing bodily peril.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberality and Miserableness (attitude toward riches)
rubrics_metrics.description: LIBERALITY: Magnanimity in the use of Riches. MISERABLENESSE / PARSIMONY: Pusillanimity regarding wealth; morally judged according to social tastes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The same disposition can be praised or blamed depending on context and degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kindness, Natural Lust, Luxury (types of love)
rubrics_metrics.description: KINDNESSE: Love of persons for society. NATURAL LUST: Love of persons for pleasing the sense only. LUXURY: Love acquired from rumination/imagination of past pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different motives produce qualitatively different loves; luxury arises from imaginative repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passion of Love and Jealousy
rubrics_metrics.description: THE PASSION OF LOVE: Love of one singularly with desire to be singularly beloved. JEALOUSIE: The same passion joined with fear that the love is not mutual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jealousy combines desire and fear; both are common human passions with social effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revengefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: REVENGEFULNESSE: Desire, by doing hurt to another, to make him condemn some fact of his own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An other-directed appetite that seeks to alter another's reputation or state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curiosity (distinctive human passion)
rubrics_metrics.description: CURIOSITY: Desire to know why and how; a passion peculiar to Man and distinguishing him from other animals; a 'lust of the mind' leading to durable delight from generating knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seen as a high human passion that sustains intellectual endeavor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion vs Superstition (fear of invisible power)
rubrics_metrics.description: RELIGION: Fear of power invisible, feigned by the mind or imagined from tales publicly allowed; SUPERSTITION: that fear not allowed. TRUE RELIGION: when the imagined power is truly such as imagined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish justified religious fear from mere superstition; true religion corresponds to actual divine power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panique Terror (crowd fear)
rubrics_metrics.description: PANIQUE TERROR: Fear without apprehension of why or what, typically arising in a throng or multitude where individuals suppose others know the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurs in crowds through contagion of fear; not truly without cause but without individual understanding of cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admiration (joy from novelty)
rubrics_metrics.description: ADMIRATION: Joy from apprehension of novelty; proper to man because it excites appetite for knowing the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linked to curiosity; novelty triggers intellectual desire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glory and Vaine-glory (confidence vs imagined abilities)
rubrics_metrics.description: GLORYING: Joy arising from imagination of one's own power/ability grounded on experience (same as Confidence). VAINE-GLORY: the same grounded on flattery of others or self-supposition (delight in consequences) rather than real ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vaine-glory begets no attempts; Confidence begets action. Vaine-glory is properly called 'vain.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Dejection (grief from perceived lack of power)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dejection: Griefe from opinion of want of power; a state of diminished hope or confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Varies with reliance on external helps; those relying on externals more prone to dejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sudden Glory (Laughter) and Sudden Dejection (Weeping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden Glory: passion causing LAUGHTER; caused by sudden acts of one's own pleasing or perceiving deformity in another by comparison. Sudden Dejection: passion causing WEEPING; caused by sudden loss of vehement hope or prop of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both are sudden motions often moderated by custom; much laughter at defects of others is a sign of pusillanimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shame (blushing) and Impudence
rubrics_metrics.description: SHAME / BLUSHING: Griefe for discovery of some defect of ability; sign of love of good reputation (commendable in youth). IMPUDENCE: Contempt of good reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shame in youth is commendable; in old age less so. Impudence is morally negative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pity (compassion) and Cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: PITTY (COMPASSION): Griefe for calamity of another arising from imagination that similar may befall oneself. CRUELTY: Contempt or small sense of others' calamity, proceeding from security of one's own fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The best men have least pity for calamities stemming from great wickedness; cruelty is absence of fellow-feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emulation versus Envy
rubrics_metrics.description: EMULATION: Griefe for success of a competitor joined with endeavour to equal or exceed him (constructive). ENVIE: Griefe for another's success joined with endeavour to supplant or hinder (destructive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish motivating rivalry (emulation) from malicious resentment (envy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberation (definition and end)
rubrics_metrics.description: DELIBERATION: When appetites, aversions, hopes, and fears concerning the same thing arise alternately and the sum continues until the thing is either done or thought impossible. Deliberation ends when the object is done or thought impossible, for until then liberty to act remains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No deliberation about past facts or things manifestly impossible; deliberation is essentially future- and possibility-oriented.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Will (last appetite of deliberation)
rubrics_metrics.description: WILL: In deliberation, the last Appetite or Aversion immediately adhering to the action (the act of Willing). Voluntary acts proceed from the Will; an 'inclination' that precedes but is not last does not make an act voluntary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntary acts may originate from appetites or aversions; definition rejects 'will as rational appetite' as inadequate because voluntary acts can go against reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of Speech expressing passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Passions can be expressed indicatively (I love, I fear), deliberation is expressed subjunctively (If this be done...); desire/aversion use imperative forms (Do this, Forbear that) which when obligatory become Command; optative for vaine-glory/indignation/pity/revenge; interrogative for desire to know (What is it?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These forms are voluntary significations but not infallible signs of passion; better signs are countenance, body motions, actions, and ends/aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good and Evil Apparent (evaluation by foresight of consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: In deliberation appetites and aversions are raised by foresight of chains of consequences; if the good in those consequences exceeds the evil, the whole chain is Apparent or Seeming Good; if evil exceeds good, Apparent or Seeming Evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One who by experience or reason has the greatest and surest prospect of consequences deliberates best and gives the best counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Felicity (definition of worldly felicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: FELICITY: Continual success in obtaining those things a man from time to time desires; continual prospering in this life. There is no perpetual tranquility while alive because life entails motion and desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish earthly felicity from beatifical vision promised in theology; felicity here is temporal and imperfect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praise and Magnification (forms of speech about worth and power)
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of speech that signifies opinion of Goodness is PRAISE; that which signifies power/ greatness is MAGNIFYING; Greek makarismos (blessing/declaring felicity) has no direct English equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are rhetorical forms used to communicate appraisal of value, power, or felicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement, Doubt, Science vs Opinion vs Conscience
rubrics_metrics.description: JUDGEMENT (final sentence) is the last opinion in enquiry about past and future (analogous to Will as last appetite). DOUBT is the whole chain of alternate opinions. Science (knowledge of consequences by discourse) gives conditional knowledge; when discourse does not start with definitions it ends in OPINION. CONSCIENCE originally meant shared knowledge of facts between people and later metaphorically private knowledge of one's own secret facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No discourse ends in absolute knowledge of fact by discourse alone; conclusions are conditional ('if this be, that will be'). Beware of treating opinion or conscience as equivalent to absolute knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief and Faith (authority vs reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: When discourse begins not at definitions but at another's saying trusted for his ability and honesty, the resolution is BELEEFE and FAITH: Faith in the person; belief both of the person and of the truth of the saying. Ecclesiastical phrasing 'believe in' indicates confession/acknowledgement of doctrine rather than mere trust in a person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Belief grounded solely on authority is faith in men or church; distinguish believing a person's report from believing a doctrine in confessional sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual Virtue: definition and comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: INTELLECTUALL VERTUE: abilities of mind prized for eminence (a 'Good Witte'); these divide into natural and acquired. Natural wit = celerity of imagining and steady direction to some approved end (speed and directedness). Acquired virtues involve method, culture, instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural wit without steadiness becomes dulness or distraction; acquired virtues require method and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good Wit / Fancy vs Good Judgement / Discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Good Wit (Fancy): observing rare similitudes and producing apt, rare metaphors—pleasing in poetry; Good Judgement: observing differences, discerning, choosing profitable actions—essential in history, demonstration, counsel. Discretion: judgement regarding times, places, persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a good poem fancy should predominate; in history judgement must predominate; orations/praise favor fancy; demonstrations and rigorous truth-seeking require judgement; metaphors are excluded in strict demonstration.
